chunks: Common characteristic impedance values. The question: What are some common characteristic impedance values?
Characteristic impedance is the fixed ratio of voltage to current for a wave traveling down a line.
A handful of standard values are used everywhere: 50 ohms for most RF and board traces, 75 ohms for video, and 90, 100 or 120 ohms for differential pairs depending on the interface.
The standard for each interface sets the number. You pick the board stackup and trace width to hit it.
Think of garden hoses and nozzles. If the hose and the nozzle are the same size, the water flows through without splashing back. If they differ, some water bounces back.
Impedance values work the same way: everything along the signal path (driver, trace, cable, receiver) should use the same standard, so nothing reflects.
The red curve (loss, normalised to its minimum) bottoms out near 77 ohms and the green curve (power handling, normalised to its maximum) peaks near 30 ohms.
At 50 ohms loss is about 1. 10 times the minimum and power is about 0. 86 times the maximum. Cable and instrument makers settled on it, and the PCB world inherited it.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): square root of L' over C' , set by the line's geometry and materials, not its length ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Differential impedance ( Z diff ): the impedance between the two traces of a pair, about twice the odd-mode impedance ("Differential pair and its tradeoffs").
Reflection coefficient ( ): the fraction of a wave that bounces back at a mismatch, (Z 2 minus Z 1) over (Z 2 plus Z 1) ("Impedance matching: what, why, when").
Tolerance: the allowed error, usually about 10 percent on a board. Controlled impedance: a board ordered with a target impedance that the fab checks on a test coupon.
A 60 ohms trace connects to a 50 ohms system. The reflection coefficient is (60 minus 50) over (60 plus 50) equals 0. 09 . So about 9 percent of the wave bounces back.
For a 10 percent tolerance, the worst case is about 5 percent. On a short trace with slow edges, you will not notice it. On a long, fast channel, small reflections add up.
That is the whole idea.
"50 ohms single-ended is the default for RF and most PCB traces, 75 ohms for video.
For differential pairs, 100 ohms is the usual value, covering Ethernet, SATA, HDMI, PCIe and LVDS, with USB at 90 ohms, and 120 ohms for CAN and RS-485.
DDR has its own 40-60 ohms single-ended values. 50 ohms comes from the coax compromise between lowest loss near 77 ohms and highest power handling near 30 ohms.
In practice the standard sets the target and I set the stackup and width to hit it within about ±10%."
